text: Thirteen delegates founded the Communist Party in Shanghai in 1921, with Soviet advice. It allied with Sun Yat-sen’s Nationalists (KMT) to unify a China split among warlords. In April 1927 the Nationalist leader Chiang Kai-shek turned on the communists and massacred thousands in Shanghai.
Many NKVD officers were themselves shot in 1938–40, including their chief Yezhov.
Most reporting focused on US soldiers; civilian deaths in the North were rarely reported.
Militant attacks had killed dozens; the leaked papers note the attacks were small and never threatened party control.
Hundreds were shot in 1959 after quick trials, and thousands overall; the numbers depend heavily on who counts.
Cuba defends the 1959 trials as justice for Batista’s torturers and does not publish totals.
Land was redistributed, but village tribunals executed thousands, many wrongly, and the party apologised in 1956.

Most people ate through the state’s Public Distribution System. From 1994 rations were cut and the northeast was largely cut off. Floods in July and August 1995 hit perhaps 30% of the country. The government called the years that followed the “Arduous March”.
Red Guards attacked officials, teachers and “bad class” families nationwide.
Law making theft of collective grain punishable by death or ten years.

China’s 1981 party resolution says the Great Leap caused serious losses. Its official yearbooks show the national death rate jumping from about 11 per thousand in 1957 to 25.4 in 1960. The party’s official history (2011) says the population fell by 10 million in 1960. It does not give a full death toll.
Almost none from inside the camps; a few smuggled videos of public executions exist. Cameras are banned.

They had little choice. The 1958 household registration rules tied farmers to their villages, and those who fled were stopped as “vagrants”. Officials who opened granaries or told the truth were struggled against, and some were beaten to death.
Detention without trial was policy; deaths came from conditions (and some killings).
Canteens ran out within months; the death rate more than doubled by 1960.
Thousands of mugshots taken by the regime’s own photographers, plus confessions and execution logs.

Commanders knew the raids were killing civilians in very large numbers and widened them, burning towns and then bombing dams. The stated targets were military. The same rating is used as for the Great Leap famine, because the test is the same: they knew, and kept going.
Hundreds of thousands to about a million died when the state food system collapsed after Soviet aid ended and floods struck; the regime first refused help.
For decades the famine was called “three years of natural disasters”. There is no national memorial; survivors and researchers such as Yang Jisheng still face censorship.
With ground forces stalemated and truce talks stalled, bombing was the pressure they could apply without more US casualties.
After Mao died in 1976, the “Gang of Four” were arrested and tried in 1980–81, and the party rehabilitated millions of victims.

In April 1975 the Khmer Rouge took Phnom Penh and emptied the cities. Money, markets, schools and religion were abolished; everyone was forced into farm labour. Educated people, officials of the old government, ethnic Vietnamese, Cham Muslims and suspected traitors were killed.

Many soldiers and guards were rural teenagers, trained to obey “Angkar” (the Organisation) without question; guards who disobeyed were killed too. Most of S-21’s prisoners were themselves Khmer Rouge cadres, tortured into confessing to being traitors.
Whether anyone was killed inside the square during the final clearing; witnesses differ, and most deaths were on the avenues.

Mao invited criticism of the party in 1956–57. When it came, he reversed course: officially 552,877 people were labelled “rightists”, and estimates of those persecuted run from one to two million. Many were sent to labour camps; at Jiabiangou in Gansu, about 2,500 of some 3,000 prisoners died.

After Batista fell on 1 January 1959, revolutionary courts tried members of his army and police accused of torture and murder. On 12 January 1959 at San Juan Hill in Santiago, 71 men were shot after summary trials and buried in a trench; reporters were present.
The same party presided over the deadliest famine in history and the largest fall in extreme poverty ever recorded. Both are true, and both belong in the story.
On 3–4 June troops opened fire on the way in; hundreds were killed.
Mao launched the campaign and approved the attacks. Most deaths came from organised repression by the army and authorities in 1968–71, according to the same local histories.
A citizens’ tribunal, not a state court, found crimes against humanity and complicity by the US, UK and Australia.
